questions.stem: Oxygen moves from the alveoli in the lungs into the blood. Which factor maintains the concentration gradient that drives this diffusion?

options.text: The heart pumping blood past the alveoli continuously
Active transport pumps in the alveolar wall
The thickness of the alveolar wall
The large volume of the lungs

questions.explanation: Blood flow constantly carries oxygen away from the alveoli, maintaining a low concentration of oxygen in the blood relative to the alveoli. This steep concentration gradient ensures continuous, rapid diffusion of oxygen. Breathing also refreshes the air in the alveoli, keeping oxygen levels high.

questions.stem: A student adds a drop of ink to cold water and warm water. The ink spreads faster in warm water. What explains this observation?

options.text: Warm water has a higher concentration of ink
Particles in warm water have more kinetic energy and move faster
Cold water is denser, preventing diffusion
Warm water has larger spaces between molecules

questions.explanation: At higher temperatures, particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more frequently. This increases the rate of diffusion. This is why diffusion is faster at higher temperatures -- the particles spread out more quickly through the random motion of the molecules.

questions.stem: The small intestine has villi with a large surface area and a rich blood supply. How do these adaptations increase the rate of diffusion of digested food molecules?

options.text: Large surface area provides more space for diffusion; blood supply maintains the concentration gradient
Large surface area traps food molecules; blood supply provides oxygen for digestion
Villi produce enzymes; blood carries away waste products
Large surface area increases temperature; blood supply provides water

questions.explanation: A large surface area means more molecules can diffuse across at the same time, increasing the overall rate. The rich blood supply carries absorbed molecules away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient (high in the intestine, low in the blood), which is the driving force for diffusion.

questions.stem: A cell is placed in a solution where the oxygen concentration outside is equal to the oxygen concentration inside. What will happen to the net movement of oxygen?

options.text: Oxygen will stop moving entirely
Oxygen will move into the cell only
Oxygen molecules will continue to move in both directions, but there will be no net movement
Oxygen will move out of the cell only

questions.explanation: When concentrations are equal (equilibrium), individual oxygen molecules still move randomly in both directions across the membrane. However, the same number move in as out, so there is no NET movement. Diffusion is the net movement from high to low concentration -- at equilibrium, net movement is zero.

questions.stem: Perfume molecules can be detected across a room within minutes. If the room temperature decreased significantly, how would this affect the time taken to smell the perfume?

options.text: It would take less time because cold air is denser
It would make no difference
It would take longer because particles move more slowly at lower temperatures
The perfume would not evaporate at all in cold conditions

questions.explanation: At lower temperatures, particles have less kinetic energy and move more slowly. This reduces the rate of diffusion, so the perfume molecules would take longer to spread across the room. The perfume would still eventually diffuse, but the process would be noticeably slower.
